strengths: WildFeedback offers a useful contribution to conversational alignment: 20,281 preference pairs constructed from naturally occurring user feedback, with a public dataset link. Connecting feedback detection, preference extraction, and response generation provides a practical resource suitable for Findings.

Training utility is supported across three model families and established benchmarks beyond the proposed checklist evaluation. For example, Phi-3’s AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate improves from 24.3% to 34.9%, and its Arena-Hard win rate improves from 15.4% to 32.4%. Regenerating UltraFeedback responses provides a more relevant comparison than relying exclusively on its original responses.

The paper includes human validation of feedback detection and checklist judgments, reports length-controlled evaluation, and explicitly separates training and test users and conversations. These are meaningful methodological safeguards.
The pipeline is clearly described, with detailed annotation rubrics, prompts, model versions, and principal training hyperparameters. These support reuse and reproduction of the main training recipe.
weaknesses: The specific benefit of extracting user feedback is not isolated. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. A control using the same WildChat prompts without preference guidance, together with an SFT-only comparison, would distinguish feedback learning from domain adaptation and GPT-4 distillation.

The strongest claims about actual user alignment exceed the validation. GPT-4o extracts preferences, generates or filters responses, and evaluates outputs using those extracted preferences. Appendix C reports 57.14% agreement with humans and kappa 0.372, versus human agreement of 63.27% and kappa 0.436. This offers partial validation, but there is no independent audit of preference-summary fidelity or human comparison demonstrating that checklists improve evaluation accuracy. Checklist compliance therefore remains an imperfect proxy for actual user satisfaction.

Claims of consistently significant superiority over UltraFeedback are overstated. In Table 3, Qwen2 trained on WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several other advantages are small, and confidence intervals or variation across training seeds are not reported.

The evaluation supports a restricted population of preferences. Selecting the most mutually similar preferences within 70 clusters deliberately emphasizes common cases; this does not establish representativeness of the broader user population. Feedback detection also has only 48.4% DSAT recall in the human validation sample. Although selection bias is acknowledged, claims about diverse, evolving preferences and reduced bias remain insufficiently demonstrated.

Some reproducibility details remain unclear, including generation settings, embeddings and precise clustering procedures, user-grouping rules, and the validation criterion for hyperparameter selection. These gaps particularly affect reconstructing the dataset and evaluation split. The resource and benchmark gains justify Findings, while the unresolved attribution and evaluation-validity questions limit the case for main-conference publication.
